subject: Imposing constraints on EFA using efaUnrotate

messages.author: 5c527df876dd0445
messages.subject: Imposing constraints on EFA using efaUnrotate
parts:
Hi,

If it makes sense at all, I just wonder if it is possible to impose a parameter constraint on EFA model using efaUrotate. I actually would like to constraint residual variances to be > 0. Is there any not-so-complicated way to do it?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Imposing constraints on EFA using efaUnrotate
parts: I actually would like to constraint residual variances to be > 0. Is there any not-so-complicated way to do it?

The EFA model syntax is automatically generated, but you can indirectly add additional constraints as model-syntax commands passed to lavaan() via the constraints argument.  If you use parTable(fit) to extract the parameter table from the unrotated lavaan object, you can see which labels lavaan generates for the residual variances.  

unrotated <- efaUnrotate(HolzingerSwineford1939, nf = 3, varList = paste0("x", 1:9))
PT <- parTable(unrotated)
PT[PT$op == "~~", ]

   id     lhs op     rhs block user free ustart exo label group plabel start   est    se

You see that the residual variances for x1-x9 are labeled ".p43." - ".p51.", so you can add inequality constraints when you run the model again.

(positiveVariances <- paste0('.p', 43:51, '. > 0'))
unrotated <- efaUnrotate(HolzingerSwineford1939, nf = 3, varList = paste0("x", 1:9),
                         constraints = positiveVariances)

However, I would not recommend constrained estimation as a solution for Heywood cases.  Constraining it potentially masks other problems with your model, and forcing negative estimates to be positive will bias other model parameters.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

Instead, test whether the Heywood case is consistent with sampling error:

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Kenneth_Bollen/publication/228937678_Testing_Negative_Error_Variances_Is_a_Heywood_Case_a_Symptom_of_Misspecification/links/00b495274eb519224c000000.pdf

If sampling error cannot be discounted (because the 95% CI includes positive values), and your model fits well, then it is reasonable to assume the Heywood case is due to sampling error rather than model misspecification.  But EFA models are exploratory models anyway, not particularly well suited to represent specific theoretical models.
